new_slides.title: A thick myelinated axon delivers one spike to the whole trunk
body: Conduction velocity depends on how quickly current spreading inside an axon can bring the adjacent stretch of membrane to threshold. A wider axon has lower internal resistance, and myelin insulates the membrane so that less current leaks out and less charge is needed per stretch.

In a myelinated axon, sodium channels cluster at the gaps between myelin segments, the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse regenerates only at the nodes and jumps between them, a process called saltatory conduction. The Mauthner axon, from the largest neuron known in the vertebrate brain, combines great width with myelin.

Fast conduction turns a long body into a nearly simultaneous target. The spike reaches the last trunk segments only slightly after the first, so the muscles of one side contract almost together and fold the body into a single C. A slow axon would contract the front of the body well before the tail, producing a traveling wave like a swimming stroke instead of a sudden turn.
transcript: Slide 4 states that the Mauthner axon is thick and myelinated, and slide 23 describes the near-simultaneous contraction of the trunk; the physics of conduction connects the two.
Two properties set conduction speed.
Current injected at one point of an axon spreads along the inside and leaks out through the membrane; the farther it spreads before leaking away, the sooner the adjacent region reaches threshold.
Widening the axon lowers the resistance along the inside, and myelin raises the resistance and lowers the capacitance across the wall, so both help the current travel farther.
Saltatory conduction concentrates the work at the nodes.
Under myelin there are few sodium channels; they are packed at the nodes, where the action potential is regenerated at full size.
The impulse therefore skips from node to node, which is both faster and metabolically cheaper than regenerating the spike continuously along bare membrane.
Speed shapes the movement itself.

Stage 1 of the C-start depends on one side of the trunk contracting as a unit, and slide 24 attributes this bend to fast, powerful contraction of segmental muscle blocks driven by the descending command.

The slower, rostral-to-caudal wave of ordinary swimming is produced by spinal circuits that activate segments in sequence, so conduction speed is part of what distinguishes an escape bend from a swimming stroke.
refs: Hecker, A., Schulze, W., Oster, J., Richter, D. O., & Schuster, S. (2020). Removing a single neuron in a vertebrate brain forever abolishes an essential behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117, 3254–3260.
Eaton, R. C., Lee, R. K. K., & Foreman, M. B. (2001). The Mauthner cell and other identified neurons of the brainstem escape network of fish. Progress in Neurobiology, 63, 467–485.

new_slides.title: Two groups of brainstem neurons time the bend and the thrust
body: In Eaton and colleagues' high-speed films, the fast body bend lasted about 20 milliseconds and moved the fish very little. Its job is to rotate the body so that the head points away from the threat; the thrust that carries the fish away comes afterward, when the tail sweeps back and pushes against the water.

The two stages are commanded at different moments. Nissanov and colleagues concluded that one group of reticulospinal neurons, which includes the Mauthner cell, sets the left-right direction and the angle of stage 1, while a second group fires about 9 milliseconds later and sets the onset and direction of stage 2.

Separate timing for turn and thrust allows the final heading to vary between escapes. Within 100 milliseconds the fish had moved 0.5 to 1.5 body lengths from their starting positions in widely varying directions, and that spread of end points makes the path of the escape hard for a predator to anticipate.
transcript: Slide 7 names the two stages of the C-start; the cited papers explain what each stage accomplishes and which neurons control its timing.
Stage 1 orients; stage 2 propels.
Eaton, Bombardieri and Meyer filmed startles at 200 frames per second in many teleost species and described the first phase as a stereotyped displacement of head and tail to one side.
A bend of this kind changes the fish's orientation much more than its position, so it acts as the aiming step of the escape.
Two neuron groups, two moments.
Nissanov, Eaton and DiDomenico combined electrical stimulation of single Mauthner cells with recordings of trunk muscle activity in swimming goldfish.

From these and earlier muscle recordings they inferred that the second group of reticulospinal neurons fires 5 to 15 milliseconds after the stage 1 cells, on average about 9 milliseconds, and determines when and in which direction stage 2 begins.
Variable trajectories are an advantage.
Eaton and colleagues described the variability of the fish's location after 100 milliseconds as adaptively unpredictable.
The muscle-timing differences described on slide 34 are the mechanism of this unpredictability, and they arise in the stage 2 command, which is the stage the Mauthner cell does not set by itself.
refs: Eaton, R. C., Bombardieri, R. A., & Meyer, D. L. (1977). The Mauthner-initiated startle response in teleost fish. Journal of Experimental Biology, 66, 65–81.
Nissanov, J., Eaton, R. C., & DiDomenico, R. (1990). The motor output of the Mauthner cell, a reticulospinal command neuron. Brain Research, 517, 88–98.
new_slides.source_line: Eaton, R. C., Bombardieri, R. A., & Meyer, D. L. (1977). The Mauthner-initiated startle response in teleost fish. Journal of Experimental Biology, 66, 65–81.

new_slides.title: Dense otoliths lag behind the body to signal sound
body: Fish tissue has nearly the density of water, so a sound wave moves the whole fish back and forth along with the surrounding water. The otolith in the saccule is a dense mineral mass that lags behind this motion, and the relative movement bends the hair bundles of the sensory cells beneath it.

Deflecting a hair bundle toward its tallest stereocilia opens mechanically gated channels and depolarizes the hair cell; deflection the other way closes them. Each hair cell therefore responds to one direction of motion, and cells oriented in different directions together encode the axis along which the water moved.

Mechanical gating opens the channels directly, with no chain of second messengers, so the ear can drive the club endings fast enough for a Mauthner spike within milliseconds. In larval zebrafish, fish lacking functional hair cells lost tap-evoked short-latency escapes while lateral-line removal left them intact, identifying the ear as their main trigger.
transcript: Slide 8 identifies the saccule as the source of the VIIIth nerve input to the lateral dendrite; how the saccule turns sound into nerve impulses explains why this channel is fast and directional.
Inertia does the detecting.
An object with the same density as water moves with the water, so a fish body is carried by the particle motion of a sound wave.
The otolith is much denser than the tissue around it, so it is slower to accelerate, and the small difference in motion between otolith and hair cells is the mechanical stimulus.
Hair cells are directional sensors.
The stereocilia of each hair cell form a staircase, and only deflection along that staircase changes the opening of the transduction channels.
This built-in orientation is one source of the directional information that slide 35 identifies as necessary for bending away from the correct side.
The ear dominates the fastest escapes.
Lacoste and colleagues tested tap-evoked escapes in mutants with nonfunctional hair cells and in fish whose lateral line had been ablated with neomycin.
Short-latency escapes depended on the ear, whereas the lateral line did not contribute to them, which fits the dominance of VIIIth nerve input on the lateral dendrite.
refs: Lacoste, A. M. B., Schoppik, D., Robson, D. N., Haesemeyer, M., Portugues, R., Li, J. M., Randlett, O., Wee, C. L., Engert, F., & Schier, A. F. (2015). A convergent and essential interneuron pathway for Mauthner-cell-mediated escapes. Current Biology, 25, 1526–1534.

new_slides.title: Chemical release at club endings grows during afferent bursts
body: Lin and Faber recorded simultaneously from a single club ending and the Mauthner dendrite, so they could follow transmission at one identified contact. When the afferent fired two or three impulses 2 to 4 milliseconds apart, the second and third chemical EPSPs were about twice as large as the first, a form of short-term facilitation.

The increase was presynaptic: the number of release sites stayed the same while the probability that each site released transmitter rose. This pattern fits the textbook account in which calcium left in the terminal after one impulse adds to the calcium entering with the following one.

Facilitation makes the chemical component sensitive to firing pattern. An abrupt, loud sound drives afferents to fire in tight bursts, so the chemical charge grows impulse by impulse, while the electrical component passes each impulse at the same strength. A burst therefore depolarizes the Mauthner cell more than the same impulses spread out in time.
transcript: Slides 10 and 11 describe the two components of the club ending synapse and the value of an adjustable chemical part; Lin and Faber's paired recordings show one way the chemical part adjusts within milliseconds.
Paired recording isolates one synapse.
Recording inside both the presynaptic club ending and the postsynaptic dendrite reveals exactly which response belongs to which impulse.
In their burst experiments the second and third EPSPs averaged 99 and 108 percent larger than the first.
Facilitation is a change in release probability.
Fluctuations in EPSP size let the authors estimate the number of release units and the probability of release, and only the probability changed during facilitation.
The number of release units was similar to the number of active zones seen in freeze-fracture images of club endings, consistent with each active zone acting as one release unit.
Some connections are silent.
Many club endings that were electrically coupled to the Mauthner cell produced no detectable chemical EPSP, even though they had the structures of chemical synapses.
Such contacts give the synapse room for later strengthening, which links this short-term plasticity to the longer-term changes in transmission described on slide 39.
refs: Lin, J.-W., & Faber, D. S. (1988). Synaptic transmission mediated by single club endings on the goldfish Mauthner cell. Journal of Neuroscience, 8, 1302–1312.
new_slides.source_line: Lin, J.-W., & Faber, D. S. (1988). Synaptic transmission mediated by single club endings on the goldfish Mauthner cell. Journal of Neuroscience, 8, 1302–1312.

new_slides.title: Spike-to-muscle timing and side make Mauthner firing causal
body: Zottoli implanted electrodes beside one Mauthner cell and recorded trunk muscle activity while free-swimming goldfish heard brief sounds. Each fish provided its own comparison: a Mauthner cell drives the opposite side of the trunk, so the recorded cell should fire before escapes powered by the far side and stay silent before escapes powered by its own side.

That prediction held. In all 34 startles powered by the muscles opposite the electrode, the spike preceded the muscle activity by 1.1 to 2.1 milliseconds, whereas the cell fired before only one of the 39 startles powered by its own side, and neither spikes nor startles occurred in another 52 tests.

The timing places the spike before the movement, and the side-specific pattern ties firing to the direction of the bend. Together they identify the Mauthner spike as the event that initiates a startle, a stronger conclusion than activity that merely accompanies startling.
transcript: Slide 14 reports a tight correlation between Mauthner firing and natural startle; the structure of Zottoli's recordings explains why the correlation supports initiation.
A crossed axon makes a built-in control.
Slide 5 explains that each Mauthner cell activates the opposite side of the body, so its firing predicts which way the fish should bend.
Recording one cell and comparing escapes in the two directions tests that prediction trial by trial within the same animal.
The numbers fit the circuit.
A delay of about one to two milliseconds between the extracellular spike and the muscle activity matches a fast descending axon with few synapses before the muscle.
The near absence of firing before escapes toward the electrode side agrees with reciprocal inhibition on slide 20, which keeps the two cells from firing together.
Free behavior links reduced preparations to real startles.
The recordings came from chronically implanted fish swimming freely, not from anesthetized or restrained animals.
This setting allows the cellular findings on synapses and inhibition be read as properties of the circuit a behaving fish uses.
refs: Zottoli, S. J. (1977). Correlation of the startle reflex and Mauthner cell auditory responses in unrestrained goldfish. Journal of Experimental Biology, 66, 243–254.
new_slides.source_line: Zottoli, S. J. (1977). Correlation of the startle reflex and Mauthner cell auditory responses in unrestrained goldfish. Journal of Experimental Biology, 66, 243–254.

new_slides.title: Low input resistance demands large, synchronous excitation
body: Input resistance sets how much a cell's voltage changes for a given synaptic current; when it is low, as in a very large neuron with a great area of membrane, a strong current produces only a small depolarization. The membrane time constant sets how long a depolarization lingers before it leaks away.

With a time constant of a few hundred microseconds, the Mauthner cell forgets an input almost at once, so separate inputs add together only when they arrive nearly simultaneously. Excitation scattered over several milliseconds, typical of ordinary background sound, decays between inputs and never sums to threshold.

Distance adds a further barrier: Lacoste and colleagues report that dendritic excitation in the adult goldfish Mauthner cell can shrink up to fourfold before it reaches the soma. An abrupt stimulus that makes many afferents fire together is the kind of input that overcomes these properties, so the passive membrane alone selects sudden events.
transcript: Slide 16 lists the cell's low input resistance, short time constant and hyperpolarized resting potential; these terms describe how a membrane converts synaptic current into voltage.
Input resistance is the voltage gained per unit of current.
A large cell has more membrane and more open channels through which current can escape, so the same current spreads out and raises the voltage less.
The Mauthner cell's size therefore makes it intrinsically hard to excite, independent of any inhibition.
The time constant sets the window for summation.
Slide 10 gives the Mauthner time constant as a few hundred microseconds, short enough that its electrical and chemical EPSP components remain separate in recordings.
The same brevity means inputs must coincide within a fraction of a millisecond to add up, which makes the cell a coincidence detector.
Three passive hurdles act together.
Lacoste and colleagues list the low input resistance, short time constant and hyperpolarized membrane as reasons the cell needs strong currents, and add attenuation along the dendrites.
Korn and Faber describe the Mauthner cell as setting the behavioral threshold of the escape, and these membrane properties are a large part of how it does so.
refs: Lacoste, A. M. B., Schoppik, D., Robson, D. N., Haesemeyer, M., Portugues, R., Li, J. M., Randlett, O., Wee, C. L., Engert, F., & Schier, A. F. (2015). A convergent and essential interneuron pathway for Mauthner-cell-mediated escapes. Current Biology, 25, 1526–1534.
Korn, H., & Faber, D. S. (2005). The Mauthner cell half a century later: A neurobiological model for decision-making? Neuron, 47, 13–28.

new_slides.title: Shunting inhibition divides excitation rather than subtracting
body: Inhibitory synapses on the Mauthner cell open channels that pass chloride ions. When the reversal potential for chloride lies close to the resting potential, opening these channels barely moves the resting voltage, but it adds many open pathways through which excitatory current leaks back out before it can depolarize the cell.

Each excitatory input then produces a smaller depolarization in proportion to how many inhibitory channels are open, so the inhibition scales excitation down rather than removing a fixed amount. A strong, synchronous input can still reach threshold, while a weak one is reduced below it.

Feedforward inhibition passes through an extra interneuron, so it arrives slightly after the direct electrical excitation. The first wave of excitation from an abrupt stimulus can reach the cell before the shunt is fully established, whereas excitation that builds slowly meets inhibition already in place, which raises the effective threshold for gradual stimuli.
transcript: Slide 17 introduces shunting feedforward inhibition; the behavior of a chloride conductance near rest explains why shunting acts as a divisor and how its timing favors abrupt stimuli.
Reversal potential decides what an open channel does.
Ions flow through an open channel toward the voltage at which their net flow stops, their reversal potential.
If that voltage is near rest, the channel causes little voltage change on its own but clamps the membrane toward rest whenever excitation tries to move it.
Division rather than subtraction.
Extra open channels lower the membrane resistance, and lower resistance shrinks the voltage produced by any given current, the same principle as the low input resistance on slide 16.
Inhibition of this kind therefore scales the response to every input by the same factor, which preserves the ranking of strong and weak stimuli while raising the bar for all of them.
Timing makes the gate selective.
The excitatory drive at the club endings includes an electrical component with essentially no synaptic delay, described on slide 10, while the inhibitory path needs at least one additional synapse.
The decision on slide 22 depends on this race: abrupt stimuli give one cell a head start before inhibition closes the gate, whereas slowly building stimuli are shunted from the beginning.
refs: Faber, D. S., & Korn, H. (1978). Electrophysiology of the Mauthner cell: Basic properties, synaptic mechanisms, and associated networks. In D. S. Faber & H. Korn (Eds.), Neurobiology of the Mauthner Cell. Raven Press.
Korn, H., & Faber, D. S. (2005). The Mauthner cell half a century later: A neurobiological model for decision-making? Neuron, 47, 13–28.
new_slides.source_line: Faber, D. S., & Korn, H. (1978). Electrophysiology of the Mauthner cell: Basic properties, synaptic mechanisms, and associated networks. In D. S. Faber & H. Korn (Eds.), Neurobiology of the Mauthner Cell. Raven Press.

new_slides.title: Spiral fibers add delayed excitation where the spike starts
body: Spiral fiber neurons, about ten on each side in larval zebrafish, cross the midline and wrap their terminals around the opposite Mauthner cell's axon hillock inside the axon cap, the site where its action potential begins. Input delivered there is not weakened by travel along the dendrites, so it carries unusual weight in deciding whether the cell fires.

Their excitation arrives about 3 milliseconds after the fast dendritic input. Lacoste and colleagues propose that this delay works as a filter: a brief, harmless sound depolarizes the dendrites only transiently, and that depolarization has faded before the spiral fiber input arrives, whereas a lasting threat keeps both inputs active long enough to coincide.

Activating spiral fiber neurons with light made weak taps 4.4 times more likely to trigger short-latency escapes and advanced them by about 1 millisecond. The axon hillock thus brings opposing signals together: spiral fiber excitation and the field-based inhibition generated in the same axon cap act on the small patch of membrane where the spike is decided.
transcript: Slide 25 introduces spiral fiber neurons as an essential second pathway; their anatomy and timing explain how they make the Mauthner decision both easier to trigger and harder to trigger by accident.
Location gives the pathway its strength.
Lacoste and colleagues found about ten spiral fiber neurons in rhombomere 3 on each side, each projecting to the contralateral Mauthner cell and apparently to no other target.
Earlier anatomical and physiological work points to both electrical and glutamatergic synapses at these terminals, the same mixed arrangement as the club endings.
A delay line can filter noise.
In goldfish, sounds produce a fast dendritic depolarization and a slower component about 3 milliseconds later, which the authors attribute to spiral fiber input.
They state that firing normally occurs 3 to 12 milliseconds after stimulus onset, so the delayed input falls inside the window in which the cell decides.
The hillock is a site of convergence.
Slide 19 describes the extrinsic hyperpolarizing potential produced in the axon cap by inhibitory interneurons, and slide 13 explains the high resistance that makes it large.
Excitation from spiral fibers and inhibition through the axon cap therefore compete at the spike initiation zone itself, making the cap a control point as well as a recording landmark.
refs: Lacoste, A. M. B., Schoppik, D., Robson, D. N., Haesemeyer, M., Portugues, R., Li, J. M., Randlett, O., Wee, C. L., Engert, F., & Schier, A. F. (2015). A convergent and essential interneuron pathway for Mauthner-cell-mediated escapes. Current Biology, 25, 1526–1534.
new_slides.source_line: Lacoste, A. M. B., Schoppik, D., Robson, D. N., Haesemeyer, M., Portugues, R., Li, J. M., Randlett, O., Wee, C. L., Engert, F., & Schier, A. F. (2015). A convergent and essential interneuron pathway for Mauthner-cell-mediated escapes. Current Biology, 25, 1526–1534.

new_slides.title: Ablation tests necessity; stimulation tests sufficiency
body: A necessity test removes a neuron and asks whether the behavior disappears; a sufficiency test activates the neuron alone and asks whether the behavior appears. The two tests answer different questions, and a neuron can pass one while failing the other.

When single Mauthner cells were stimulated electrically, stage 1 angular velocity averaged 22% lower than in sensory-evoked starts, and the stage 2 turning angle 47% smaller. One Mauthner spike is enough to start an escape and set its direction, while the full escape also uses reticulospinal neurons that a natural stimulus recruits at the same moment.

Each test is only as complete as its manipulation. Lesions that leave part of a neuron working test a partial removal, and an electrode that fires one cell tests that cell stripped of its usual partners. The Mauthner case turned on both points: incomplete lesions explain the escapes that survived, and isolated stimulation explains the weaker ones.
transcript: Slides 26 to 28 frame the command-neuron question and the experiments used to answer it; separating the two halves of the definition shows what each experiment could and could not test.
Two halves of one definition.
Kupfermann and Weiss defined a command neuron as one that is both necessary and sufficient for a behavior, and the two parts require opposite manipulations.
Slide 27 is a necessity test, and slide 28 is a sufficiency test, so their results speak to different parts of the definition.
Stimulation revealed a partial sufficiency.
In Nissanov and colleagues' measurements, the distance moved during stage 2 also fell by 15% for electrically triggered starts.
They concluded that two groups of reticulospinal neurons act together, the Mauthner cell's group setting direction and stage 1, the other setting stage 2.
Lesion completeness decided the necessity result.
Hecker and colleagues showed that escapes survive soma loss only as long as the axon's initial segment survives, as slide 29 describes.
Testing necessity properly therefore required confirming the state of the axon in each animal, which is what overturned the earlier interpretation.
refs: Nissanov, J., Eaton, R. C., & DiDomenico, R. (1990). The motor output of the Mauthner cell, a reticulospinal command neuron. Brain Research, 517, 88–98.

Hecker, A., Schulze, W., Oster, J., Richter, D. O., & Schuster, S. (2020). Removing a single neuron in a vertebrate brain forever abolishes an essential behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117, 3254–3260.
new_slides.source_line: Nissanov, J., Eaton, R. C., & DiDomenico, R. (1990). The motor output of the Mauthner cell, a reticulospinal command neuron. Brain Research, 517, 88–98.

new_slides.title: The axon initial segment, not the soma, sets escape speed
body: An axon separated from its cell body undergoes Wallerian degeneration: deprived of proteins made in the soma, it breaks down over the following hours to days. Hecker and colleagues followed this process in individual zebrafish larvae and tested escapes at each stage, from intact cell to soma lost, initial segment lost and whole axon lost.

While the axon initial segment survived, larvae still made fast escapes, though less often. Once it degenerated, short-latency escapes vanished and turning speed collapsed, even when the rest of the axon remained. The initial segment is where spikes start and where spiral fiber input arrives, so it is the only point at which inputs can still reach an axon without its soma.

The two compartments therefore do different jobs. The soma and its large dendrites gather sensory evidence and set how often an escape is released, while the initial segment converts that decision into the spike that sets latency and turning speed. Soma lesions removed the first job and left the second working.
transcript: Slide 29 explains that the Mauthner axon can outlive its soma; Hecker and colleagues' staged comparisons identify which part of the surviving axon carries the escape.
Degeneration proceeds in stages.
The authors used two-photon laser irradiation to remove the soma and then imaged the same larva repeatedly as its axon degenerated, testing escapes in between.
The time at which the initial segment disappeared varied by at least 20 hours among larvae, so the stage of degeneration, not the time since the lesion, predicted performance.
Two measures, two compartments.
Response probability dropped as soon as the soma was lost, whether or not the initial segment remained.
Latency and angular speed stayed fast until the initial segment was lost, after which the only starts left were slow ones.
A single entry point for inputs.
Spiral fiber neurons terminate on the axon hillock, as slide 25 describes, so their input survives soma loss as long as the initial segment does.
The authors point out that, for the intact cell, all relevant inputs can therefore be monitored from the soma, which makes the Mauthner cell a bottleneck through which the escape decision must pass.
refs: Hecker, A., Schulze, W., Oster, J., Richter, D. O., & Schuster, S. (2020). Removing a single neuron in a vertebrate brain forever abolishes an essential behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117, 3254–3260.
new_slides.source_line: Hecker, A., Schulze, W., Oster, J., Richter, D. O., & Schuster, S. (2020). Removing a single neuron in a vertebrate brain forever abolishes an essential behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117, 3254–3260.

new_slides.title: Mixed predator trials isolate the survival cost of one neuron
body: Hecker and colleagues placed each predator with eight larvae: four lacking both Mauthner axons and four untreated larvae that could be told apart afterward under fluorescence. Sharing a container meant that every larva faced the same predator, hunger level and space, so differences in capture came from the larvae themselves.

Two controls removed the obvious alternatives. Sham larvae received the same laser treatment aimed at two cerebellar neurons and survived like untreated larvae, so the procedure alone did not make fish easy prey, and groups of untreated larvae from the two strains used survived equally well.

The larvae without Mauthner axons were the ones captured. Earlier arguments held that shaving about 4 milliseconds off latency moves a fish only a few millimeters and could not matter; against a predator that strikes ballistically at a target, those milliseconds decide whether the strike lands on the fish or on the spot it has just left.
transcript: Slides 30 and 31 report that losing the Mauthner axon reduced survival against a real predator; the structure of the predation experiment explains why that conclusion is secure.
Mixed groups equalize the encounter.
Each container held one hungry predator and a mix of treated and untreated larvae, and survivors were counted every hour over a 7-hour session.
At the end, fluorescence identified which survivors were ablated and which were controls, so the analysis compared the two kinds of larvae within the same encounters.
Controls rule out the procedure and the strain.
Sham ablation of cerebellar neurons used the same laser energy, and these larvae survived as well as untreated ones.
Homogeneous groups of each strain survived similarly, so the difference cannot be traced to genetic background.
Latency matters against targeted strikes.
The authors suggest that short-latency starts may help little against suction-feeding predators, so the survival value depends on the kind of attack.
The few milliseconds separating Mauthner-driven from slower starts, described on slides 15 and 27, are exactly the margin that matters when a strike is aimed at where the fish is.
refs: Hecker, A., Schulze, W., Oster, J., Richter, D. O., & Schuster, S. (2020). Removing a single neuron in a vertebrate brain forever abolishes an essential behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117, 3254–3260.
new_slides.source_line: Hecker, A., Schulze, W., Oster, J., Richter, D. O., & Schuster, S. (2020). Removing a single neuron in a vertebrate brain forever abolishes an essential behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117, 3254–3260.

new_slides.title: Serial copies of the Mauthner cell give a slower backup
body: The embryonic hindbrain develops as a row of repeated segments called rhombomeres, and several classes of neurons recur in neighboring segments as serial copies of one another. MiD2cm and MiD3cm are such copies of the Mauthner cell: they share its crossed descending axon and auditory input but are smaller cells in the segments behind it.

Smaller size changes performance. A thinner axon conducts more slowly, and the homologs have different thresholds, so the escapes they drive start later and turn less sharply. When Lacoste and colleagues removed the Mauthner cells, most tap-evoked escapes shifted from short latency to long latency, 13 to 25 milliseconds, rather than disappearing.

Serial duplication gives the hindbrain a graded set of escape triggers. The Mauthner cell provides the fastest and most powerful start, and its homologs a slower route that still moves the fish away, which is why losing the Mauthner cell lengthens and weakens escapes long before it removes the ability to flee.
transcript: Slides 32 and 33 introduce MiD2cm and MiD3cm and compare their escapes with Mauthner escapes; the segmental origin of these cells explains why they resemble the Mauthner cell and why they are weaker.
Segmentation produces families of similar neurons.
Each rhombomere produces a comparable set of reticulospinal neurons, so a neuron in one segment often has counterparts in the adjacent ones.
Lacoste and colleagues refer to two sets of such segmental homologs that are thought to drive longer-latency escapes when the Mauthner cell does not fire.
Latency classes reveal which cells drove an escape.
In their larvae, escapes of 12 milliseconds or less were classed as short-latency and those of 13 to 25 milliseconds as long-latency.
Removing the Mauthner cells shifted escapes toward the long-latency class without changing the overall probability of responding.
Backup is real but imperfect.
Hecker and colleagues found that once the Mauthner axon was gone, the starts that remained were all of substantially longer latency, and these did not protect larvae from a predator.
The homologs therefore preserve the ability to move away while losing the speed that gives Mauthner-driven escapes their survival value.
refs: Lacoste, A. M. B., Schoppik, D., Robson, D. N., Haesemeyer, M., Portugues, R., Li, J. M., Randlett, O., Wee, C. L., Engert, F., & Schier, A. F. (2015). A convergent and essential interneuron pathway for Mauthner-cell-mediated escapes. Current Biology, 25, 1526–1534.

Hecker, A., Schulze, W., Oster, J., Richter, D. O., & Schuster, S. (2020). Removing a single neuron in a vertebrate brain forever abolishes an essential behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117, 3254–3260.
new_slides.source_line: Kimmel, C. B., Eaton, R. C., & Powell, S. L. (1980). Decreased fast-start performance of zebrafish larvae lacking Mauthner neurons. Journal of Comparative Physiology, 140, 343–350.

new_slides.title: Habituation differs from fatigue and from sensory adaptation
body: Habituation is a learned decline in response to a repeated stimulus that predicts nothing. Two other processes can also reduce responding: sensory adaptation, in which receptors become less responsive, and motor fatigue, in which muscles or motor neurons can no longer respond fully.

Two tests separate them. A habituated response recovers at once when a different strong stimulus is presented, called dishabituation, which fatigued muscles could not do; and habituation to one sound leaves the response to a different sound intact, which would fail if the whole startle machinery were exhausted.

In the Mauthner circuit, weaker transmission at the club endings and stronger inhibitory synapses both lower responsiveness, but at different points: the first reduces the sensory drive reaching the cell, and the second raises the excitation needed to fire it. Both leave the cell able to fire a full spike, so experience moves the decision threshold while the command stays intact.
transcript: Slide 39 describes habituation of the startle and plasticity at excitatory and inhibitory synapses; separating habituation from other causes of reduced responding shows where in the circuit each change acts.
Three ways a response can fade.
Sensory adaptation lies in the receptors, fatigue lies in the motor output, and habituation lies in the connections between them.
Only habituation depends on learning that the stimulus carries no threat.
Dishabituation and stimulus specificity are the diagnostic tests.
A novel or strong stimulus restoring the response indicates that the motor system can still perform.
Specificity to the repeated stimulus places the change in the pathway carrying that stimulus rather than in the animal's general state.
Plasticity at both sides of the threshold.
Lin and Faber found many club endings with electrical coupling but no detectable chemical transmission, showing that the chemical part of these synapses can vary in strength.
Korn and Faber emphasize that plasticity at the Mauthner cell's synapses and networks keeps the escape appropriately unilateral, variable and unpredictable.
refs: Korn, H., & Faber, D. S. (2005). The Mauthner cell half a century later: A neurobiological model for decision-making? Neuron, 47, 13–28.
Lin, J.-W., & Faber, D. S. (1988). Synaptic transmission mediated by single club endings on the goldfish Mauthner cell. Journal of Neuroscience, 8, 1302–1312.

new_slides.title: Co-active brainstem neurons shape what a Mauthner spike does
body: A Mauthner spike contracts the opposite side of the trunk, yet an S-start bends the body into an S rather than a C. The difference must come from what else is active at the same moment: other reticulospinal neurons and spinal circuits that contract the front and the back of the body on opposite sides.

Stimulation experiments point the same way. A Mauthner spike evoked on its own produced a weaker stage 1 bend and a smaller stage 2 turn than a natural escape, so every natural fast start already takes part of its shape from companion neurons recruited together with the Mauthner cell.

The Mauthner cell supplies the speed and timing of a fast start, and the surrounding brainstem network specifies its shape and direction. Recruiting the same trigger for a feeding strike gives prey capture the same short latency that makes escape effective, an advantage when the prey can itself dart away.
transcript: Slide 40 reports that the Mauthner cell fires during S-start prey capture as well as C-start escape; combining this with the stimulation results explains how one cell can contribute to two movements.
Shape comes from the ensemble.
An S-shaped bend requires opposite sides of the front and back of the body to contract together, which a single crossed axon acting alone does not produce.
Additional descending neurons active at the same moment are the most direct way to add the second bend.
The Mauthner cell works inside a network.

Eaton, Lee and Foreman describe the Mauthner cell as one member of a parallel brainstem escape network in which the pattern of activity across neurons sets the timing and size of muscle contractions on each side.
Nissanov and colleagues' finding on slide 28 that isolated stimulation gives weaker starts is the escape-side evidence for the same arrangement.
One fast trigger, several uses.
Canfield and Rose recorded Mauthner activity during the feeding strike, so the cell's speed serves approach as well as avoidance.
A strike that starts within milliseconds reaches prey before it can react, the mirror image of an escape that starts before a predator's strike arrives.
